claims.text: The file is a coordinated set rather than a single report, and the node should cite it item by item: Blue Book final case report, 13 November 1968, twelve pages; Basic Reporting Data, 28 October 1968, eight pages, prepared by Lt Col Arthur J. Werlich, 862nd Combat Support Group Operations Division; the 91st Strategic Missile Wing Security Controller's summary of UFO observers at Launch Control Facilities with sighting times; the Base Operations Dispatcher's Log for 0800 to 1010Z recording ground reports from site N-7; seven AF Form 117 questionnaires; thirteen B-52 ASQ-38 radarscope photographs at 8x10 with data plates; the Werlich overlay map at 1:200,000; upper-air rawinsonde data; and a transcription of recorded conversations between the B-52 co-pilot and Radar Approach Control.

The seven AF Form 117 respondents are named in the file: A1C Lloyd M. Isley and A1C Robert Michael O'Connor of the 91st MIMS; A1C Joseph Patrick Jablonski, A1C Gregory Adams, SSgt James Frederick Bond and SSgt William E. Smith Jr. of the 862nd SPS; and Major James A. Partin, pilot, 23rd Bomb Squadron, 5th Bomb Wing. The B-52H crew at the debriefing was co-pilot Capt. Bradford Runyon, radar navigator Maj. Charles Richey, navigator Capt. Patrick McCaslin, electronic warfare officer Capt. Thomas Goduto and gunner TSgt Arlie Judd.

claims.text: SECTION 2a PROVENANCE, AND THIS CASE IS THE CONTROL GROUP FOR THE WHOLE CLUSTER. The modern investigation exists because one of the B-52 crew, Capt. Bradford Runyon, contacted the Center for UFO Studies in 2000 on his own initiative and completed a CUFOS questionnaire. A witness approached a research body; a research body did not recruit a witness. That is the opposite of the pattern that dominates the Malmstrom material, and it is why this case carries the weight it does.

desc: The best-instrumented nuclear-site incursion case in the American record, and the one where the number of independent detection channels is the argument. In the early hours of 24 October 1968, about thirty miles northwest of Minot AFB, North Dakota, USAF ground radar tracked an unidentified object correlated with an orange glow and passed it to the crew of a B-52H, call sign JAG 31, at 2,000 feet on a 290-degree heading: a target at the one o'clock position at 24 miles at about 3:30 a.m. CDT, 15 miles by 3:35 a.m., and by 3:52 a.m. also being tracked by base weather radar at 3 miles. At 3:58 a.m. Minot requested IFF transponder identification and the B-52H's radio transmitter failed for four minutes. The bomber's own radar tracked a bright red-orange object, and the object was reported down at a location logged as 'AA-43' for some forty-five minutes. Simultaneously, Minuteman ICBM launch facilities of the 91st Strategic Missile Wing designated N, O, J and M Flights reported sightings and electromagnetic effects including security alarms triggered at both the outer and inner rings of a silo, an outer door opened and the combination lock of an inner door moved. Named witnesses include Maj. Bradford Runyon, S/Sgt Bond and S/Sgt Smith. Dan Wilson located 108 documents on the case and NARCAP found 141. Project Blue Book did not send field investigators, and Jan Aldrich's assessment of the Blue Book file is that the Air Force obfuscated the case badly enough that the obfuscation itself is visible in the paper. Richard Haines analysed the B-52H radar imagery. Minot 1968 is the case where the phrase 'threat to a primary nuclear offense system' is not rhetoric: radio failure, radar correlation and physical security breaches at a nuclear launch facility on the same night.
